title: Trauma primary survey (ATLS)
summary: Order the ABCDE by what kills fastest, and treat the chest, shock and fluid traps the exam sets.
closing: Airway first, treat what kills in minutes, reassess whenever the patient changes.

objectives.text: Pick the first step in the primary survey and put ABCDE in order by speed of killing, not by visibility
Decide what to do next for a patient who is talking, and when to repeat the airway check; pick GCS 8 or less as the trigger for a definitive airway
Choose the emergency surgical airway for an adult versus a child under 12
Treat tension pneumothorax at once by clinical diagnosis, with needle decompression before X-ray or ventilation, at the site the exam expects
Tell tension pneumothorax from massive haemothorax and cardiac tamponade by neck veins, percussion, trachea and Beck's triad
Recognise the early sign of haemorrhagic shock, the class where hypotension appears, and the cases that mislead (neurogenic, child, elderly, beta-blocker)
Choose the initial fluid volume and type, and the target in brain injury versus haemorrhage
Send an unstable patient to FAST not CT, and pick the urethrogram before catheterisation
State that the secondary survey and AMPLE history begin only after the primary survey and resuscitation
Give the antifibrinolytic and its time window in bleeding trauma
Name the three peaks of trauma death and the one ATLS targets

traps.trap: Haemorrhage is the leading preventable death, so control bleeding before securing the airway (also absorbs TR13: xABCDE / MARCH order carried into an ATLS question)
A patient who talks is fully safe, so the primary survey can stop there
Tension pneumothorax needs a chest X-ray before decompression
An unstable trauma patient goes to CT for abdominal bleeding (also absorbs TR24: FAST treated as confirming organ injury)
Ventilate or intubate the tension pneumothorax patient before decompressing
Hypotension with bradycardia in trauma is haemorrhagic shock
Tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax look the same on examination
Beck's triad belongs to tension pneumothorax
Hypotension appears early in haemorrhage (Class II)
Initial crystalloid bolus is 2 L in adults (old PYQ key; Ringer-lactate-only variant TR12 handled in feedback)
Needle decompression goes in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, in adults
Paradoxical chest-wall movement causes the hypoxia in flail chest
Tracheal deviation points toward the injured side in tension pneumothorax
Normal vital signs exclude shock in children, the elderly, pregnancy and beta-blocked patients
Surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency airway for a child
Insert a urinary catheter first to check for urethral injury
The third peak (sepsis, days to weeks) is the window ATLS targets
A chest injury list for the primary survey is any chest injury, including simple pneumothorax and rib fractures, with tamponade left out
Permissive hypotension is the target in traumatic brain injury
Tranexamic acid works up to 8 hours
